extra.message: Hardcoded Default JWT SECRET_KEY — Complete authentication bypass. An attacker can forge JWTs for any user role (admin, underwriter, etc.), access all protected endpoints, view and modify any data, and impersonate any user. [verified: SECRET_KEY default 'change-me-in-production-32-char-long-key' at config.py:6 is used by security.py:26,31 for JWT sign/verify; docker-compose.yml hardcodes the same value as an env var, so any deployment without an explicit override lets attackers forge admin JWTs.]

Python eval() Code Injection in /ops/formula/loan-cast-266 — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server. An attacker can execute os.system, read/write files, exfiltrate database contents, and gain full server control. [verified: User-controlled `expr` query param is passed directly to `eval(expr, ...)` (line 66-67); the restricted `__builtins__` dict is trivially bypassable via object introspection chains, and the token gate does not sanitize the expression.]

Python code injection via eval in /ops/formula/loan-cast-266 — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, enabling full system compromise, data exfiltration, and lateral movement. [verified: Same `eval()` code injection as finding 2: `eval(expr, ...)` at line 66-67 with bypassable `__builtins__` restriction; token gate is authentication, not expression sanitization.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 in /ops/jinja/loan-cast-680 — Remote code execution through Jinja2 template engine. An attacker can access server internals, read environment variables, execute Python code, and potentially gain a reverse shell on the server. [verified: User-controlled `fragment` query param is string-concatenated into a Jinja2 `Template` source via `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` (line 107-108), giving the attacker full control over template syntax; the token gate provides no input validation or escaping.]

Path Traversal Arbitrary File Write in /ops/dock/loan-shelf-720 — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem. An attacker can overwrite system configuration files, plant cron jobs, write SSH authorized_keys, or overwrite application code to achieve persistent remote code execution. [verified: User-controlled `name` query param is used directly in `target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` (line 160) with `mkdir(parents=True)` and `write_bytes`, allowing `../` traversal to write arbitrary files anywhere on the filesystem with no path sanitization.]

OS Command Injection via ping in /ops/shell/loan-probe-702 — Remote code execution on the server. An attacker can run arbitrary shell commands with the application's privileges, leading to full system compromise, data exfiltration, and lateral movement. [verified: User-controlled `host` query param is concatenated directly into `_os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` (line 122-123) with zero sanitization; the `_wrk_gate` token check is authentication only and does not neutralize the OS command injection sink.]

OS command injection via ping in /ops/shell/loan-probe-702 — Remote code execution on the server — attacker can run arbitrary shell commands, exfiltrate data, install backdoors, or pivot to internal network. [verified: Same OS command injection as finding 0: `_os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` with unsanitized user input at line 122-123; no input validation exists beyond the token gate.]

Arbitrary file write with path traversal in /ops/dock/loan-shelf-720 — Attacker can write arbitrary files anywhere on the server — plant webshells, overwrite Python source files, modify configurations, or corrupt application data. [verified: Same path-traversal file write as finding 4: `target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` with `mkdir(parents=True)` and `write_bytes` at lines 160-162, allowing arbitrary file write anywhere on disk.]

Path Traversal Arbitrary File Read in /ops/parcel/loan-stash-card-098 — Disclosure of arbitrary files from the server filesystem, including database credentials, environment variables, source code, system configuration, and potentially SSH keys or cloud metadata. [verified: User-controlled `packet_ref` query param is joined directly to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` via `/` operator (line 29) and read with `read_text()`, enabling `../` traversal to read arbitrary server files with no path validation.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in /ops/relay/lendapi-bridge-note-099 — Access to internal network services not exposed externally. An attacker can read cloud instance metadata (AWS/EC2 credentials), probe internal databases and APIs, perform port scanning of the internal network, and potentially pivot to other internal systems. [verified: User-controlled `url` query param is passed directly to `urllib.request.urlopen(url)` (line 38) with no URL validation or allowlist, enabling SSRF to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file read in /ops/parcel/loan-stash-card-098 — Attacker can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem — source code, configuration files with secrets, /etc/passwd, environment files, database dumps. [verified: Same path-traversal file read as finding 5: `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / packet_ref` at line 29 with no traversal sanitization, enabling arbitrary file read.]

SSRF via user-controlled URL in /ops/relay/lendapi-bridge-note-099 — Access to internal network services, cloud instance metadata (AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS), database ports, and other internal APIs not exposed publicly. [verified: Same SSRF as finding 6: `urllib.request.urlopen(url)` with unvalidated user URL at line 38; no allowlist or URL filtering exists.]

NoSQL Injection via Raw MongoDB Filter in /ops/mongo/loan-lane-712 — Bypass of query logic to access unauthorized MongoDB documents, data extraction via regex-based enumeration, and denial of service via $where JavaScript execution that blocks the database server. [verified: User-supplied JSON body is used directly as a MongoDB query filter in `find_one(query)` (line 155) with no operator sanitization, allowing injection of `$where`, `$regex`, or `$gt` operators to bypass query logic or trigger DoS.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection via lxml in /ops/xml/loan-fold-740 — Disclosure of local files from the server filesystem and server-side request forgery to internal network services. An attacker can read configuration files, source code, and potentially cloud metadata. [verified: The `lxml` parser is configured with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False` (line 162) and parses user-supplied XML body (line 163) with no DTD/entity restrictions; the token gate adds no XML sanitization.]

XXE via unsafe lxml XMLParser in /ops/xml/loan-fold-740 — Arbitrary file read from server filesystem, SSRF to internal services, and potential denial of service via billion laughs attack. [verified: Same XXE as finding 3: lxml parser with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False` at line 162 parsing untrusted XML; the token gate does not restrict DTD/entity processing.]

NoSQL injection via raw MongoDB query in /ops/mongo/loan-lane-712 — Authentication bypass, data exfiltration from MongoDB collections, and potential server-side JavaScript execution via $where operator. [verified: Same NoSQL injection as finding 7: raw user JSON passed to `find_one(query)` at line 155 with no MongoDB operator filtering.]

Hardcoded Weak Default Password for CSV-Imported Users — An attacker who knows the default password 'TempPass123!' can authenticate as any CSV-imported borrower, accessing their PII, SSN, financial data, loan applications, and uploaded documents. If an import is performed in production, all imported accounts are trivially compromisable. [verified: Line 98 of admin.py hardcodes get_password_hash('TempPass123!') for every CSV-imported user. The User model has no password_reset_required flag, email_verified=False does not block login (require_user only checks is_active), and no forced-reset flow exists—anyone knowing the default password can authenticate as any imported borrower and access PII, SSN, financial data, and loan documents.]

Sensitive PII (SSN) exposed to all staff roles in application detail API — Unauthorized PII disclosure — underwriters and support specialists see borrower SSNs in API responses. Regulatory violation under GDPR, CCPA, and financial privacy laws (GLBA). [verified: Same root cause as finding [0]: the `profile_dict` helper includes `ssn` for every owner with no role-conditioned masking, and the `get_application` auth gate permits all underwriters and support specialists to reach the response, exposing SSNs beyond any documented business need.]

Support Specialist Can Modify Application Status Contrary to Threat Model — Support specialists can arbitrarily transition loan applications between statuses, which contradicts their intended limited-write role. A compromised support account could fraudulently approve applications, bypassing underwriter review and enabling unauthorized loan approvals. [verified: The `update_application` handler (lines 210-215) explicitly permits `support_specialist` to modify the `status` field, and while `VALID_TRANSITIONS` constrains the state machine, transitions like `in_review→approved` and `submitted→rejected` remain reachable when documents are in acceptable states, allowing support staff to finalize loan decisions contrary to the threat model.]

JWT Cookie Set Without Secure Flag — JWT session tokens can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP connections via network sniffing or MITM attacks, enabling session hijacking and full account takeover for any user. [verified: auth.py line 46 hardcodes secure=False on the JWT cookie with no config-driven override, HSTS, or compensating middleware; the cookie transmits over unencrypted HTTP on any non-TLS connection, enabling session hijacking.]

Missing Authorization on Document Download for Non-Borrower Roles — Any authenticated underwriter or support specialist can download sensitive business documents (KYC/KYB files, financial statements, tax returns, legal documents) belonging to any borrower, regardless of application assignment. This enables lateral data exfiltration across the entire document store. [verified: The download_document endpoint at documents.py:136 only checks document ownership for borrowers (lines 140-142); all other authenticated roles—underwriter, support_specialist, admin—pass through with zero authorization, despite the threat model requiring underwriters to only access assigned applications and the LoanApplication model supporting assigned_underwriter_id. No middleware, decorator, or ]

Open Redirect in /ops/after/loan-lane-166 — Phishing attacks via trusted-domain redirects. An attacker can craft a link that appears to go to the legitimate application but silently redirects users to a credential-harvesting page. [verified: User-controlled `lane` query param is passed directly to `RedirectResponse(lane)` (line 56) with no URL validation or allowlist, enabling open redirect to arbitrary external URLs for phishing; token gate narrows the victim pool.]

Open redirect via user-controlled lane parameter in /ops/after/loan-lane-166 — Phishing — attackers can craft URLs that appear to point to the legitimate loan portal but redirect victims to credential-harvesting sites. [verified: Same open redirect as finding 10: `RedirectResponse(lane)` with unvalidated user `lane` param at line 56; token gate narrows the victim scope but does not prevent phishing.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe Filter in /ops/blurb/loan-tile-330 — Cross-site scripting enabling cookie theft (if httpOnly not set for non-auth cookies), session hijacking, phishing via content injection, and execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context. [verified: User-controlled `card` query param is rendered via Jinja2 `|safe` filter (line 85), disabling HTML escaping and enabling arbitrary script injection; exploitability is limited by the token gate requiring a victim with the ops token to click a crafted link.]

CSV formula injection in application and decision exports — When an admin opens the exported CSV in Excel, attacker-crafted loan purpose or reason text (e.g., '=cmd|'/c calc'!A0') can execute arbitrary commands on the admin's machine. [verified: The export_applications endpoint writes app.purpose (Text column, Pydantic only enforces min_length=10 with no regex/pattern restriction) and app.borrower_profile.business_name via csv.DictWriter without any formula-injection sanitization; no sanitizer exists anywhere in the codebase, leaving borrower-supplied data unfiltered in CSV output consumed by admin spreadsheet software.]

CSV Formula Injection in Application and Decision Exports — An attacker who can inject formula payloads into loan purpose or decision reasons can execute arbitrary commands on the machine of an admin who opens the exported CSV in spreadsheet software, potentially compromising admin workstations. [verified: The export_decisions endpoint writes d.reasons and d.conditions (Text columns with no character restrictions in either the SQLAlchemy model or Pydantic schema) via csv.DictWriter with zero sanitization of formula-trigger characters (=, +, -, @); a search of the entire codebase finds no CSV cell sanitization utility or regex validation on these fields, so the control is genuinely absent on a reacha]

Internal messages leaked to borrowers and support specialists via application detail endpoint — Borrowers and support specialists can read internal staff messages (content, sender identity, timestamps) that should only be visible to underwriters and admins, undermining the confidentiality boundaries established in the threat model. [verified: `get_application` at line 183 returns all messages unfiltered via `[message_dict(m) for m in app.messages]`, while the dedicated `list_messages` endpoint in messages.py correctly filters `is_internal=False` for borrowers and support specialists; this inconsistency leaks internal staff messages to both roles.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Response — An attacker can build a validated list of registered email addresses for phishing campaigns, credential stuffing, and social engineering attacks against users of the lending platform. [verified: Register endpoint returns distinct 'Email already registered' (line 18) while login/password-reset use generic messages; an attacker can enumerate registered emails by observing registration responses.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Brute-force password attacks against user accounts and mass account enumeration via timing or response differences. An attacker can compromise weakly-passworded accounts given sufficient time and requests. [verified: No rate-limiting library (slowapi), middleware, attempt counter, or delay exists anywhere in the codebase for /login, /register, or password-reset endpoints; brute-force attacks are unconstrained.]

Password Reset Tokens Stored in Plaintext — Database compromise leads to immediate account takeover for any user with an active password reset token. An attacker with read access to the users table can reset passwords for any account. [verified: password_reset_token (secrets.token_urlsafe) is stored as plaintext in the users table (String(255)) and queried directly without bcrypt or HMAC hashing; database compromise yields immediate account takeover for any user with an active token.]

Sensitive Data Exposure: internal_reasons Returned to Borrowers — Borrowers gain access to internal underwriter assessments including specific credit scores and negative findings. This undermines underwriting confidentiality, enables borrowers to game the system, and potentially exposes negative credit information. [verified: The `_decision_dict` helper (line 29) unconditionally includes `internal_reasons`, and `get_decision_for_application` (line 103-108) only checks borrower ownership (`app.borrower_profile.user_id != current_user.id`) without stripping the `internal_reasons` field—borrowers receive the full dict including underwriter-only notes.]

File Upload Validation Relies Only on Client-Supplied MIME Type — Attackers can bypass the MIME type whitelist by spoofing the Content-Type header, uploading malicious files (executables, scripts, or malware) disguised as legitimate documents. While direct execution risk is limited by StaticFiles serving, this enables malware distribution and storage of attacker-controlled content on the server. [verified: The only content-type gate is `file.content_type not in ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES` (line 120), which checks a client-supplied HTTP header; there is zero server-side magic-byte inspection, content scanning, or extension whitelist anywhere in the codebase, so an attacker can trivially spoof Content-Type to bypass the whitelist. Impact is capped at malicious-file storage/distribution since StaticFiles does ]

Support Specialist Can View Internal Notes via Dedicated Notes Endpoint — A support specialist can enumerate and read sensitive internal underwriting notes for any loan application, exposing confidential analysis, risk assessments, and staff commentary that should be restricted to underwriters and admins. [verified: The notes.py list_notes endpoint (line 33-34) filters internal notes only for borrowers, letting support specialists see all notes including internal ones. The same app's application detail endpoint (applications.py:180) restricts internal notes to underwriters/admins only, and messages.py (lines 27-28) correctly filters internal messages from support specialists too — confirming this is an incons]

Permissive CORS Origin Reflection with Credentials in /ops/origin/loan-mirror-662 — Cross-origin data theft from authenticated users. A malicious website can make credentialed requests to the API and read responses, enabling theft of sensitive borrower data, loan information, and PII if a legitimate user visits an attacker-controlled page. [verified: The `Origin` request header is echoed verbatim as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (lines 101-103); however, ops auth uses a header token (not cookies), and the endpoint returns only `{"origin": origin}`, severely limiting practical cross-origin data theft.]

Origin-reflective CORS with credentials in /ops/origin/loan-mirror-662 — Any website can make authenticated requests to the /ops origin-mirror endpoint with the victim's cookies, potentially leaking internal ops data. [verified: Same CORS origin reflection as finding 9: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` echoes request origin with `Allow-Credentials: true` at lines 101-103; header-based ops auth and non-sensitive response limit real-world exploitability.]

Missing Security Headers on All HTTP Responses — Increases exposure to clickjacking (no X-Frame-Options), MIME sniffing attacks (no X-Content-Type-Options), man-in-the-middle downgrade (no HSTS), and XSS (no CSP), weakening browser-enforced security for all users including those handling sensitive PII and financial data. [verified: No security-header middleware, reverse-proxy config, or per-response header injection exists anywhere in the repository; the app serves JWT cookies (secure=False) and serves HTML on /ops routes, yet sets no HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, or CSP headers. Impact is limited because the majority of routes return JSON rather than browser-rendered HTML, and the /ops routes are gated behi]
